Beyond Value Functions: Single-Loop Bilevel Optimization under Flatness Conditions

Liuyuan Jiang, Quan Xiao, Lisha Chen, Tianyi Chen

Read the paper ↗Code ↗Video & storyboardCite

PBGD-Free / The takeaway

Use one update per level instead of repeated inner solves.

Bilevel training can require refining a lower-level model component repeatedly before updating the upper-level decision. PBGD-Free replaces that nested procedure with one lower-level tracking step and one upper-level update per iteration. Its flatness condition describes when this simplification is valid: the outer loss changes little as the lower variable moves near an optimum.

The updateOne step per level

Each iteration updates the lower variable once and then the upper variable, removing the extra solve used to track the lower-level minimum value.

↘Why it worksNear-optimum flatness

A bound on how much the outer loss changes near a lower optimum controls the bias from skipping the value-function correction. Definition 1.

↘Language-model fine-tuningLower evaluated losses

With the same training-time budget, Llama-3-3B preference loss is 0.7837 versus 0.8055 for ALRIGHT. Supervised loss is 0.8516 versus 0.8656. Lower is better. Table 2.

01The idea

Learn a preference backbone while a head adapts.

The decision

In the paper’s LLM application, x contains LoRA parameters in the backbone and y is the output head. The head learns supervised fine-tuning (SFT); the backbone is guided by direct preference optimization (DPO) through that adapted head.

The bottleneck

A full penalty gradient estimates both the original SFT-optimal head and a perturbed head. Dropping the value-function correction saves one response estimate, but the removed term is multiplied by the penalty and can remain important.

The idea

Upper-level flatness bounds how the DPO objective varies around an SFT-optimal head. Together with the lower-level regularity conditions, it controls the stationarity error of one lower update followed by one outer update.

1

Original and perturbed responses

Value-function-based methods track an original lower-level response alongside a perturbed response. Those are different optimization tasks.

2

The response retained by PBGD-Free

PBGD-Free keeps the perturbed lower-level tracking update and uses the upper partial gradient. It removes the response needed solely for the value-function correction.

3

Flatness bounds the omitted correction

The flatness inequality bounds upper-loss variation around the original lower-level response. Theorem 3 uses that condition to quantify the bias and residual introduced by the simplified update.

How the method works

  1. 01

    Identify a flat upper objective

    Bound how the upper loss changes when y moves away from a lower-level solution.

  2. 02

    Drop the value-function loop

    Use the upper partial gradient in the simplified PBGD-Free update.

  3. 03

    Control the remaining bias

    Analyze convergence with the flatness parameters and the paper’s other assumptions.

Flatness controls the bias from omission

Removing the value-function correction saves a response computation. The omitted term creates a bias, which the analysis bounds using upper-level flatness.

In practice

Preference learning and backbone reuse

The application separates preference learning in the backbone from supervised adaptation in the head. The second evaluation phase asks whether the learned backbone remains useful when only the head is trained for a new task. This is why the paper reports both the original outcome and post-SFT behavior.

Flatness controls the remaining bias

Flatness controls the bias left by the omitted correction. The convergence bound combines a decaying iteration term with a residual determined by the flatness parameters.

Proposition 2

Omission can leave a persistent bias

Under generic Lipschitz conditions, Proposition 2 identifies a non-vanishing stationarity residual after omitting the correction. This motivates the flatness condition used to control the bias.

Read the statement ↗
Theorem 3

Convergence with a flatness floor

Under Assumption 2, uniform exponent 1 < α\alphaα ≤ 1.5, the stated penalty and step sizes, and an averaged trajectory flatness residual δ\deltaδ, the theorem bounds average squared penalty-gradient norm by a decaying iteration term plus a flatness-dependent floor, as displayed above. Lemma 3 separately relates penalty stationarity to the original problem under its accuracy conditions.

Read the statement ↗
Reasoning behind the formulation

The penalty magnifies response error

The difference between original and perturbed lower-level responses enters the penalty gradient with a factor γ\gammaγ. Controlling the resulting bias requires the upper-loss sensitivity captured by flatness.

Flatness measures upper-loss sensitivity

Definition 1 states ∣f(x,yg∗(x))−f(x,y)∣≤c∥yg∗(x)−y∥α+δ|f(x,y_g^*(x))-f(x,y)|\leq c\lVert y_g^*(x)-y\rVert^\alpha+\delta∣f(x,yg∗​(x))−f(x,y)∣≤c∥yg∗​(x)−y∥α+δ. The residual δ\deltaδ permits local variation, while α\alphaα controls how the distance contribution shrinks near a lower-level optimum. The paper generally studies δ\deltaδ > 0 and α\alphaα > 1.

Flatness enters the convergence bound

The single-loop method tracks the perturbed lower response and updates x using ∇xf\nabla_x f∇x​f. Theorem 3 combines flatness with lower-level regularity to quantify the stationarity error and its residual.

The outer direction is the upper partial gradient; the original value-function correction is omitted under the analyzed flatness conditions.

Assumptions behind the analysis

The convergence analysis combines smoothness, lower-level PL-type conditions, the flatness parameters, and algorithmic step-size choices. It quantifies stationarity error and the bias from omitting the value-function term. See Definition 1 and the convergence results in Section 3.

Definition 1 · Section 3 in the paper

Questions

What does flatness measure?

Definition 1 measures upper-loss variation around a lower-level optimum using a distance exponent and a residual. The residual allows local variation, and the theorem carries its contribution into the stationarity bound.

How does the method extend to constraints?

This paper analyzes the unconstrained setting. The broader efficient-penalty preprint develops fixed-set and coupled-constraint extensions. The coupled method retains an inner solve for its constrained response.

Related projects

The efficient-penalty preprint extends the smoothness analysis and flatness-based updates to fixed and coupled constraints.
